summary: A glossary of terminology used in routing requirements and solutions for Low-Power and Lossy Networks, composed of many resource-limited embedded devices. It helps keep terminology consistent across related documents.

plainLanguage.summary: A word list for networks of tiny gadgets with weak batteries.

subtitle: Standardized terminology for routing in networks of tiny, power-constrained devices.

tldr.problem: Networks of embedded devices with limited power and memory (such as sensor networks and building automation systems) use specialized routing concepts. Different researchers and vendors used inconsistent terms for the same devices and mechanisms, causing confusion in standards work.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7102 provides a glossary of 50+ standardized terms for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs), including device types (sensors, actuators, field devices), routing concepts (DAG, RPL, multipoint-to-point), and application domains.
tldr.outcome: All IETF routing documents for LLNs (such as RPL and ROLL requirements) now use these shared definitions, enabling clear technical communication across different application areas.

facts.label: Typical data rates
facts.value: A few kilobits to hundreds of kilobits per second

today: RFC 7102 is Informational. Its terminology is used in all IETF ROLL and routing-related documents concerning LLNs. As LLN deployments have grown (especially in IoT and industrial settings), the standardized vocabulary has become essential for interoperability and clear technical communication.

sections.title: What Are Low-Power and Lossy Networks?
sections.content:
A Low-Power and Lossy Network (LLN) is a collection of many small embedded devices connected by radio links, with severe constraints on power, memory, and processing capacity. These networks power real-world applications: temperature and humidity sensors in building HVAC systems, industrial equipment monitoring, home lighting control, power meter reporting, environmental monitoring, and more.

An LLN device might have kilobytes of RAM, tens of kilobytes of Flash memory, and a 8- or 16-bit processor. Many run on batteries and sleep for long periods to conserve power. Radio links are lossy—packets sometimes fail to arrive—and have limited bandwidth, often just a few tens of kilobits per second.

Because these devices are very different from traditional routers and servers, they need specialized routing approaches. The IETF Routing Over Low-power and Lossy networks (ROLL) working group developed terminology to describe these approaches consistently across different application domains.
sections.plainLanguage: Sensor networks are networks of tiny, battery-powered gadgets with weak radios. They work differently from regular routers, so they need their own vocabulary.

sections.title: Field Devices: Sensors, Actuators, and Routers
sections.content:
An LLN is built from field devices: physical devices placed in the network's operating environment. Field devices include sensors (devices that measure something—temperature, pressure, light—and report it), actuators (devices that control something—a valve, switch, or motor), and routers (devices that relay traffic for others).

A sleepy node is a field device that saves power by sleeping (radio off, processor halted) for periods and waking up to listen for messages. A non-sleepy node always stays powered on. Sleepy nodes are common in battery-powered sensors; non-sleepy nodes are common in plugged-in equipment or nodes that must respond immediately.

An LLN Border Router (LBR) connects the LLN to the outside world (the Internet, a company network, or a central control system). It runs standard IP routing and translates between the LLN's specialized routing protocol and wider networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Field devices are the tiny machines. Some sleep to save batteries, some stay awake. The border router is the gateway connecting the tiny network to the big one.

sections.title: Routing Model: DAG and RPL
sections.content:
LLN routing often builds on a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)—a network structure with no loops where traffic flows toward a root (usually the LBR). A RPL (Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks) is the main IETF protocol for LLNs that builds and maintains this structure.

In RPL, traffic patterns are naturally asymmetric. Multipoint-to-Point (MP2P) traffic flows upward from many sensors to a central data sink (the LBR): a temperature reading from a sensor in the warehouse to the control center. Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) traffic flows downward from the root to many nodes: a command to all lights in a building to turn on. Point-to-Point (P2P) traffic goes between any two nodes, often requiring multi-hop paths.

The root of the DAG typically computes rank values (hop count or cost) that determine the forwarding structure, ensuring efficient paths without loops.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages usually flow up to a central hub (like reports to a manager) or down from it (like orders to workers). The network structure is a tree with no circles.

sections.title: Application Domains and Use Cases
sections.content:
LLNs are deployed in diverse domains, each with different requirements. Building automation controls heating, ventilation, air conditioning, lighting, fire alarms, and access. Devices are often plugged in but still power-conscious. Industrial monitoring observes equipment health and processes, sometimes in harsh environments. Smart Grid applications (Advanced Metering Infrastructure, Distribution Automation) manage electrical generation, transmission, and consumption. Connected home includes appliances, security, and home automation. Healthcare monitors patients and environmental conditions. Environmental monitoring tracks pollution, weather, and wildlife.

Each domain has different trade-offs: Industrial applications may tolerate higher latency but need high reliability. Smart metering requires infrequent but reliable message delivery. Building automation often allows longer response times but must cover large areas.
sections.plainLanguage: These networks are everywhere: controlling your office building's temperature, reading your electric meter, monitoring a factory, or watching weather. Each has its own priorities.

sections.title: Terminology for Consistency
sections.content:
RFC 7102 defines terms consistently so that when a specification says 'sleepy node' or 'non-sleepy node,' all engineers understand the same thing. Terms are grouped by concept: basic devices (field device, sensor, actuator), network devices (LBR, DAG, RPL), infrastructure terms (channel, timeslot, schedule), and application categories (building automation, industrial, Smart Grid).

The glossary explicitly excludes application-specific terminology to keep it broadly useful across all LLN domains. It is intended to be referenced by all IETF routing documents that involve LLNs, making standards work clearer and reducing ambiguity.
sections.plainLanguage: One consistent vocabulary across all tiny-network standards so everyone talks about the same thing.
